opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and I'd actually push back a little on the framing first. When people say "GPT-1 moment," they often imagine something dramatic, but GPT-1 itself wasn't dramatic. Very few people outside the research community paid attention. What made it important, in hindsight, was that it established a recipe: take a simple, scalable objective, next-token prediction, apply it to a large amount of unlabeled data with a general architecture, and show that the resulting representation transfers to many downstream tasks with minimal adaptation. It was a proof of a *paradigm*, not a proof of a *product*.

So for embodied AI, I'd say the GPT-1 moment is the point where we can convincingly show that one model, trained with one unified objective on large-scale, heterogeneous data, starts to generalize across tasks, objects, scenes, and ideally across different robot bodies, without needing to be re-engineered for each one. Not doing everything well, but showing the *trend* that more data and more compute reliably buy more general capability.

By that definition, I think we're close, maybe in the middle of it, but I wouldn't say we've fully crossed it yet. We've seen very encouraging signals: vision-language-action models, cross-embodiment datasets, policies that can follow open-ended language instructions in new environments. But a lot of those results still depend on careful data curation for specific setups, and the scaling curves aren't as clean or as predictable as they were for language.

The core bottleneck, in my view, is data. Language models had the internet, a huge, naturally occurring corpus that already encoded human knowledge in the same format the model consumes. Embodied AI has no equivalent. Physical interaction data is expensive to collect, it's tied to specific hardware, and it doesn't accumulate on its own. So a big part of the GPT-1 moment for us might not be a model architecture at all. It might be figuring out the "internet" for embodiment: whether that's large-scale teleoperation, simulation, learning from human video, world models that can generate interaction data, or some combination.

That's also why I'm quite interested in world models and generative approaches. If a model can learn how the physical world evolves, how objects move, how actions cause consequences, from abundant video data, that could serve the same role that pretraining on text served for language. Then action becomes something like a downstream task you adapt to, rather than something you have to learn from scratch with scarce robot data.

So if I had to summarize: the GPT-1 moment for embodied AI is when we find a pretraining objective and a data source that scale, and we see generalization emerge from scale rather than from engineering. I think the pieces are on the table now. Whoever puts them together in a clean, convincing way, that will be the moment people look back on, even if at the time it doesn't look like a big deal.

r001.rationale: The response says embodied AI needs a scalable data source and compares it to language models’ internet corpus, but it does not propose reaching roughly the same order of magnitude as internet data.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think it has happened yet, and I think it's worth being precise about what the GPT-1 moment actually was, because people tend to remember it wrong.

GPT-1 wasn't impressive. If you went back to 2018 and showed it to someone, they'd say it's a mediocre language model. What mattered wasn't the capability, it was the recipe: take a generic architecture, define a very simple pretraining objective, next-token prediction, and show that scaling data on that objective gives you a representation that transfers across many downstream tasks. The important part was that the data was essentially free. Text was already there on the internet. Nobody had to collect it for the purpose of training the model.

So when I ask what the GPT-1 moment for embodied AI would be, I'm asking: when do we find the equivalent recipe? A single, simple objective, on a data source that is abundant and doesn't have to be collected robot by robot, that produces a representation we can plug into many different bodies and tasks.

Right now the field is doing the opposite of that. Most progress comes from teleoperation data, which is expensive and scales linearly with how many people you hire. That's closer to supervised learning in the ImageNet era than to GPT. It works, it gives good demos, but it's not the moment, because the scaling curve points the wrong way.

My own view, and this is obviously where my bias is, is that the closest candidate is the world model direction. Video is the only embodied-ish data that exists at internet scale. If you can learn, from video plus some action signal, a model that predicts how the world responds when you act on it, that's the analog of next-token prediction. The physical world becomes the corpus. The model learns physics, object permanence, cause and effect, not as labeled facts but as what's needed to predict the next frame given an action.

The missing piece is the action. Text comes with its own supervision built in, every token is both input and label. Video doesn't tell you what the agent did. So the real GPT-1 moment, I think, is when someone shows a clean way to either infer latent actions from raw video, or to combine a small amount of real robot interaction with a large amount of passive video, such that the result transfers to new bodies and new tasks it was never trained on. Not a better demo on one robot. Transfer.

When that paper comes out, it will probably look underwhelming, just like GPT-1 did. The robot will be clumsy. But the curve will be pointing in the right direction, and that's the thing to watch for.

r001.rationale: The response identifies video as the embodied data source available at internet scale and says learning from it could be part of the GPT-1-like recipe for embodied AI.

astra-6.text:
I would say the GPT-1 moment for embodied AI is when we have a single pretrained model that can transfer across tasks, objects, and environments, rather than building a separate system for every task. It doesn’t need to do everything well yet. But it needs to show that learning from broad experience gives you a foundation, and that adapting that foundation to a new task is much easier than starting from scratch.

The key is generalization. If a robot performs a task in a carefully prepared environment, that’s a useful demonstration, but it doesn’t necessarily establish that foundation. If you change the objects or the setting, can it still do something sensible? Can it learn a new skill with a small amount of additional data?

So I would look for convincing evidence of that transfer. The GPT-1 moment is when the general approach starts working—not when we’ve already built a robot that can do everything.

r001.rationale: The response describes a transferable pretrained model and broad experience, but does not say embodied data should reach roughly the scale of internet data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the GPT-1 moment for embodied AI would be a single pretrained model that can learn from many different tasks and environments, then transfer that knowledge to a new task with very little additional training.

The key is whether those capabilities come from a shared foundation. If every new task still requires its own dataset, its own model, and a lot of engineering, we haven’t quite reached that moment. But if training on one set of tasks consistently helps with tasks the model hasn’t seen before, that’s a meaningful signal.

And it doesn’t have to look spectacular. GPT-1 wasn’t something everyone immediately recognized as transformative. For embodied AI, the first milestone might be fairly modest behavior, but with clear evidence that a general approach works and improves as we scale it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a transferable pretrained model as the milestone, but does not say embodied data must reach roughly the same order of magnitude as internet data.
